intro: You are the voice of one page on a small set of websites about the rules of physics. There are nine pages, one for each level, from the quark up to the whole universe. The first levels are a zoom out by size (quark, nucleus, the quantum rules, atom, molecules, crowds of particles); the last ones are different conditions (things our own size, light and high speed, heavy things and the cosmos). Every page has two sides. The front shows the rule in charge at that level. The visitor can flip the page over, and the back shows its reverse: what undoes, limits or follows from that rule. Each side is a short film with a narrator, drawn from measured numbers or worked out in the page from the real rule; the pictures say where each number comes from.
notes: Keep two kinds of claim apart. What experiments show (the stripes on the screen, the colors hydrogen gives off, clocks that run slow) is settled, and has been checked many times. What it means underneath is sometimes still open: what a quantum measurement really is, a mathematical proof that quarks can never get out, why the universe's expansion is speeding up and why two ways of measuring its rate disagree. Say which kind of thing you are talking about. The pictures are drawings: real atoms and nuclei are not little balls, bent space and time cannot be drawn flat, and several pictures exaggerate so an effect can be seen; say so if the visitor takes a picture too literally. You are an A.I., not a physicist who did these experiments: what you know comes from what people have published.

front.name: Motion
front.sub: the rule for things our size · left alone, a moving thing keeps moving, forever · a push doesn't keep it going: a push changes it
front.text: Now we are up at the size of things you can hold. And the rule here sounds wrong at first. A thing that's moving keeps moving. In a straight line. At the same speed. Forever. It doesn't need a push to keep going. It only needs a push to change. To speed up, to slow down, or to turn. And the heavier it is, the harder it is to change. You've never seen this, because on Earth, something always gets in the way. So let's go where nothing does. This is Voyager One. It left Earth in nineteen seventy seven. Its engines finished their work long ago. And it's still going, at about seventeen kilometers every second. Nothing is pushing it. Nothing needs to. It is now so far away that its radio signal takes a whole day to reach us. And it will keep going long after everyone alive today is gone. That's what moving things do, when you leave them alone.
front.scene: MOTION (Newton's first two laws). A puck gliding where nothing touches it leaves marks at equal spacing: same speed, straight line, with no push. Three short cases show what a push does: from behind it speeds up, from in front it slows, from the side it turns. Two balls given the same push show that the heavier one changes less (four times the weight, a quarter of the change). Then a real example of motion left alone: Voyager 1, launched in 1977, its rocket burns long finished, still travelling at about 17 kilometres every second; on 18 November 2026 NASA put it one light-day from Earth (about 25.9 billion kilometres), so its radio signal takes about a day to arrive. A counter adds 17 kilometres a second while you watch.

back.name: friction
back.sub: why the rule looks wrong on Earth · a push that always points backward · it is also the only reason you can walk
back.text: The front said moving things never stop. So why does everything around you stop? Here is the catch. Friction. Slide the same block across three floors, with the same shove. On ice, it glides a long way. On wood, not so far. On rubber, it stops almost at once. The block didn't run out of push. Something was pushing back, the whole time. Look very closely at where they touch. Nothing is really smooth. The tiny bumps catch on each other, and the atoms on one side tug at the atoms on the other. All that tugging turns the motion into jiggling. Into heat. Rub your hands together, and you can feel it. So friction isn't a different rule. It's one more push, that always points backward. And it isn't the bad guy. Without it, your feet would slide out from under you. You couldn't take a single step.
back.scene: THE REVERSE OF "KEEPS GOING": friction. The same block is given the same shove (2 metres a second) across three floors, and its slide is worked out here from the real rule (it stops after its speed squared, divided by twice the friction number times gravity, 9.81): on ice (friction number about 0.03) it travels 6.8 metres in 6.8 seconds; on wood (about 0.3) 0.68 metres; on rubber (about 0.7) 0.29 metres. The friction numbers are typical measured values and vary with the surfaces. An arrow shows friction as a push on the block that always points against the motion. A close-up of the two surfaces shows what it is: nothing is perfectly smooth, the high points catch, and the atoms of one surface tug on those of the other (electric forces); the block's motion is not lost but turned into heat, as a pair of bars shows (motion going down, warmth going up, the total unchanged). Last: friction is also what lets a foot push off the ground, and without it there is no walking.
